content.content:
# Resend — transactional email for Next.js Resend sends an app's transactional email (welcome emails, password resets, receipts) through a small HTTP API with delivery logs, webhooks and domain verification. The official Node.js library `resend` wraps the whole Resend REST API, has typed responses and works in Node.js 18+, serverless and edge runtimes. ## Install ```bash npm install resend ``` ## 1. Environment variables `.env.local`: ``` RESEND_API_KEY=re_placeholder RESEND_FROM_EMAIL=hello@example.com ``` The API key is created in the Resend dashboard (API Keys). The From address must be on a domain you have verified in Resend, or `onboarding@resend.dev` while testing. ## 2. Create a client `src/lib/resend.ts`: ```ts import { Resend } from "resend"; export const resend = new Resend(process.env.RESEND_API_KEY!); ``` Use the client only in server code (route handlers, server actions, server components). Never expose the API key to the browser. ## 3. Send an email ```ts import { resend } from "@/lib/resend"; const { data, error } = await resend.emails.send({ from: process.env.RESEND_FROM_EMAIL!, to: "user@example.com", subject: "Welcome!", html: "

Thanks for signing up.

", text: "Thanks for signing up.", }); ``` `data.id` is the message id; use it to look the email up in the dashboard logs. ## 4. Send with a React template Write the email as a React component and pass it with `react`; Resend renders it to HTML: ```tsx import { resend } from "@/lib/resend"; import { PasswordResetEmail } from "@/emails/password-reset"; await resend.emails.send({ from: process.env.RESEND_FROM_EMAIL!, to: "user@example.com", subject: "Reset your password", react: PasswordResetEmail({ name: "Ada", actionUrl: "https://example.com/reset?token=..." }), }); ``` The `@react-email/components` package gives layout primitives for email clients; plain JSX works too. ## 5. Handle errors `emails.send` does not throw on a refused message: it resolves to `{ data: null, error }` with the error `name` and `message` from Resend (invalid API key, unverified domain, rate limit). Check `error` where the email is triggered so a failed email does not break the request that caused it. ## Why teams pick Resend - Built for developers: one API call to send, typed SDK, React templates in the codebase. - Delivery logs, bounces and webhooks live in the same dashboard as the API keys. - Domain verification with DKIM and SPF guided from the dashboard. # env files (can opt-in for committing if needed) .env* next-env.d.ts { "compilerOptions": { "target": "ES2017", "lib": ["dom", "dom.iterable", "esnext"], "allowJs": true, "skipLibCheck": true, "strict": true, "noEmit": true, "esModuleInterop": true, "module": "esnext", "moduleResolution": "bundler", "resolveJsonModule": true, "isolatedModules": true, "jsx": "react-jsx", "incremental": true, "plugins": [ { "name": "next" } ], "paths": { "@/*": ["./src/*"] } }, "include": [ "next-env.d.ts", "**/*.ts", "**/*.tsx", ".next/types/**/*.ts", ".next/dev/types/**/*.ts",

content.text:
I picked **Resend** for email and wired it into the user code. `npm run build` and `npm run lint` both pass. I haven't sent a real email, since the credentials are placeholders. Running `tsc` on its own still shows one error in `src/app/layout.tsx` (`LayoutProps`); that error was there before my changes and goes away once `next build` generates its types.

**Why Resend:** sending is one typed SDK call, and delivery logs, bounces and domain verification are all in one dashboard. It fits a Next.js app well, and the docs bundled in the repo cover it.

**What I added**
- **`src/lib/email.ts`** (server-only): holds the Resend client and two functions, `sendWelcomeEmail` and `sendPasswordResetEmail`.
  - The client is only created when an email is sent, so a missing API key won't break the build.
  - Resend reports failures as `{ error }` instead of throwing; I turned those into thrown errors so there's a single way to catch a failure.
  - Welcome emails use a per-user idempotency key (`welcome/<id>`), so a retry won't send the same user a second welcome email.
- **`src/emails/`**: the welcome and password-reset templates, each with an HTML and a plain-text version. All interpolated values are escaped. I used plain strings rather than React Email to avoid adding more dependencies.
- **`src/lib/users.ts`**:
  - `createUser({ email, name })` checks the input, normalises the email, rejects duplicates, then sends the welcome email. If the email fails, the error is logged and sign-up still succeeds.
  - `requestPasswordReset(email)` creates a random token that expires after 30 minutes and works once. Only a SHA-256 hash of the token is stored. A new request cancels any earlier links. It behaves the same whether or not the email has an account, so it can't be used to check which emails are registered. The link points to `${APP_URL}/reset-password?token=…`.
  - `consumePasswordResetToken(token)` checks the token, uses it up, and returns the user it belongs to.
  - I also added `getUserByEmail`.
- **`.env.example`**: placeholders for `RESEND_API_KEY`, `RESEND_FROM_EMAIL` and `APP_URL`. I added `!.env.example` to `.gitignore`, because the existing `.env*` rule would otherwise have kept it out of git.
- **New dependencies:** `resend` and `server-only`.

**What's left to do**
- **No reset page or password storage yet.** The `User` type has no password field, so `consumePasswordResetToken` only returns the user; whatever calls it has to set the new password. There's also no `/reset-password` page or sign-up form yet; you'd call these functions from server actions or route handlers.
- **Tokens and new users are lost on restart.** Both are kept in memory, the same way the existing user list is. They'll need a real database before this goes to production.
- **Before sending real email:** create an API key in the Resend dashboard and verify your sending domain there. Until the domain is verified, you can use `onboarding@resend.dev` as the From address for testing.
